summary: Sally-Ann Delucia introduces Alyx, Arize's AI agent harness with 40+ skills for building AI applications, built on the Arize observability platform. Alyx must analyze the very trace/span data it generates, creating a unique context management challenge framed as context engineering rather than prompt engineering. The core principle: the best context strategy lets an agent remember what it needs and forget what it doesn't. The team fell into a vicious loop: Alyx runs on span data, spans grow, context limit is hit, Alyx fails, retries with more data, fails again. Three approaches were tried. Naive truncation (first 100 characters, drop the rest) broke reasoning—follow-ups looked like new conversations. Summarization via LLMs was too inconsistent with no control over what was deemed important. Smart truncation with a memory store became the working solution: keep the head (first 100 chars) and tail (last 100 chars), truncate the middle, store the middle in retrievable memory. This has been stable for months. For long sessions, the team implemented evals loading 10 turns and testing the 11th. Sub-agents emerged as a game-changer: the main conversation stays light, heavy data-intensive operations are delegated to sub-agents whose results pass back to the main agent. Ongoing challenges remain: very large prompts still hit provider limits, long-term memory is absent (users increasingly push to 20+ turns and want to reference prior conversations across chats), and context selection is still a heuristic with no principled context budget or clear quality metrics. The team found that Claude Code uses a similar truncation and compression strategy, offering no secret shortcut. Key takeaways: context engineering matters, memory matters, evaluation matters, and agents don't fail because of prompts—they fail because of context. In Q&A, the team noted they store context in a database with IDs and Alex retrieves via a tool that previews messages, but caching sophistication is a future investment; long-term memory is the current priority based on user complaints.

sections.title: Introduction and speaker background
sections.summary: Sally-Ann Delucia introduces herself as Head of Product at Arize with a data science background. She is a core contributor to Alyx, functioning as both PM and part-time AI engineer, and speaks from firsthand experience of the pain of building agents.

sections.title: Overview of Alyx
sections.summary: Alyx is an AI harness built on Arize's observability platform with advanced planning, 40+ skills, and core workflows including prompt optimization, data generation, augmentation, and annotations. Speaker directs interested listeners to the booth for demos.

sections.title: Context engineering vs. prompt engineering
sections.summary: The shift from prompt engineering to context engineering is framed via a Karpathy reference. Context engineering is strategically choosing what the model sees, not just fitting data under a token limit. Context management is framed as both a product/UX problem and an engineering one.

sections.title: The vicious loop of data growth
sections.summary: Alyx was built using Alyx, creating a vicious loop: Alyx runs on trace/span data, spans grow, context limit is hit, Alyx fails, retries with more data, fails again. The system analyzing the data was constrained by the data itself.

sections.title: Why naive truncation failed
sections.summary: The first approach kept the first 100 characters and dropped the rest. It worked for simple tasks but broke reasoning: follow-ups looked like new conversations. Over-truncation caused the agent to forget everything.

sections.title: Why summarization proved unreliable
sections.summary: Summarization via LLMs seemed obvious but was too inconsistent. There was no control over what was important—leaving the LLM to decide what to keep was unreliable, so this approach was also abandoned.

sections.title: The solution: Smart truncation and memory stores
sections.summary: The working solution combines head/tail truncation with a retrievable memory store: keep first 100 characters (head) and last 100 (tail), truncate the middle, store the middle so the agent can retrieve it when needed. This gives the agent control over what context matters and has been stable for months.

sections.title: Long session challenges and evaluation
sections.summary: Users don't restart chats, so conversations grow and failures appear late. The team implemented long session evals: load 10 turns and test the 11th to understand how context management performs. This makes context bugs testable rather than waiting for user reports.

sections.title: Offloading tasks to sub-agents
sections.summary: Even with smart truncation and evals, too much data can overwhelm one agent. The solution is sub-agents: the main conversation stays light with chat and light context only, while heavy data-intensive operations are delegated to sub-agents. Results pass back to the main agent, and the memory store remains accessible. This has been a game-changer and the team has rolled out many sub-agents for data-intensive operations.

sections.title: Ongoing challenges and future work
sections.summary: Huge context still breaks things; very large prompts hit provider limits. Since Alyx operates on agent data, customer context growth compounds the problem. The recurring pattern is sub-agents—breaking things up. Long-term memory is absent and actively being built: conversations have grown from under 10 turns to 20+ turns, and users want to reference prior issues across new chats. Context selection remains a heuristic with no principled context budget or quality metrics; evals are the main measurement tool.

sections.title: Findings from the Claude Code source release
sections.summary: The team examined the Claude Code source release hoping for a secret strategy. Surprisingly, Claude Code uses a similar truncation and compression strategy to what Arize landed on—no hidden shortcut was found.

sections.title: Final key takeaways
sections.summary: Context management is iterative—everyone should keep learning. Three things are clear: context engineering matters, memory matters, and evaluation matters. Agents don't fail because of prompts, they fail because of context. In the early days prompts were everything; now the focus is squarely on context engineering.

sections.title: Q&A session
sections.summary: An audience member asks about Claude Code's effort to avoid invalidating cache with context management. The team currently stores context in a database with IDs; Alex has a tool with all IDs and previews of where in the conversation to access. More sophisticated caching is a future investment, but current focus is on long-term memory since that generates the most user complaints.
